summary: Help 7–9 year-olds understand how rainforest animals are adapted to survive, always chaining FEATURE → FUNCTION → SURVIVAL. Cover camouflage (leaf insects, tree frogs hide), warning colours/aposematism (poison dart frogs advertise toxicity), prehensile tails (some monkeys, such as spider and howler monkeys, grip canopy branches with their tails), specialised beaks (toucans reach distant fruit) and nocturnality (often avoiding predators or finding food, and for some animals avoiding daytime heat or drying out). Tie each adaptation to a rainforest layer, and contrast camouflage (hide) against aposematism (advertise) as opposite tricks that both aid survival. The core objective is causal: a feature is not decoration — the right trait in the right layer can make the difference between surviving and not (being eaten, falling, or going hungry).
misconceptions: 'Bright colours help animals hide' — opposite: aposematic colours ADVERTISE toxicity as a warning.
'Animals choose to adapt / decide to change' — adaptations are inherited traits shaped over generations, not a lifetime choice.
'Camouflage means invisible' — it works against the RIGHT background and against a predator's vision, not absolutely.
'A tail is just for balance' — a prehensile tail actively grips like a hand.
'All rainforest animals are active in the day' — many are nocturnal to avoid heat and predators.

activities.title: Predator's-eye survival scenarios
steps: Place a leaf-mimic insect onto a bright red flower, then predict whether a hunting bird will spot it; move the same insect onto a matching green leaf and predict again, then check which one the bird is more likely to spot and catch in this scene.

Meet a poison dart frog with blazing blue/red colour; predict what happens if its colour is dulled to try to hide it, then compare with keeping it bright and watch whether the predator approaches or veers away.

Give a spider monkey its prehensile tail and watch it wrap the tail round a high branch to hang and reach for fruit, then remove the tail in the model and see it can no longer hang by its tail, so it must cling with hands and feet and reaching far becomes riskier — connecting the feature to surviving in the canopy.
For each animal, state the FEATURE, the FUNCTION it does, and the SURVIVAL problem it solves, and say which rainforest layer it lives in.
Before each reveal, predict what happens if the feature is missing or wrong (predict-then-check).
activities.insight: A feature such as colour, tail or beak is not decoration: the right trait in the right layer can make the difference between surviving and not — avoiding being eaten, holding on, or getting food. Hiding (camouflage) and shouting 'I'm poisonous' (aposematism) are opposite tricks doing the very same job — staying alive. Camouflage works against the RIGHT background and a predator's vision, not absolutely.

activities.title: Feature → function reference gallery
steps: Explore each adapted animal and reveal the survival job its feature does: camouflage = hide, warning colour = deter predators, prehensile tail = grip, big light beak = reach distant fruit, nocturnal = avoid predators and find food (for some, avoid daytime heat).
For each hotspot, note which rainforest layer the animal belongs to (e.g. a spider monkey's prehensile tail in the canopy, a leaf insect camouflaged among understory or canopy leaves).
Use a same-animal-two-backgrounds image to see camouflage working on one background and failing on another.
activities.insight: Each feature pairs with a specific function and survival benefit, and each animal sits in a particular rainforest layer. This anchors the abstraction to real named animals.

activities.title: Match and contrast end-check
steps: Match each adaptation to the benefit it provides (camouflage→hide, warning colour→deter, prehensile tail→grip, beak→reach food, nocturnal→avoid predators/find food, for some avoid heat).
Answer a contrast question: given a described animal, decide whether it survives by HIDING (camouflage) or by being SEEN (warning colours), and explain why.
Name a specific animal for each adaptation and its rainforest layer.
activities.insight: Learners can distinguish the opposite strategies of hiding versus advertising, and connect real animals to their adaptation, benefit and layer.

activities.title: Explain the dart frog paradox (discussion probe)
steps: Consider: a poison dart frog is bright, shining red — one of the easiest things to spot in the forest. Explain why a frog would be coloured that way when it makes it so easy to see.
Explain how that is different from a leaf insect's dull, blending colours.
Answer the extension: what will a predator do next time it sees a bright frog after once eating one and getting sick, and how does that protect other frogs?
Discuss: if a harmless frog were also bright red but NOT poisonous, could that still help it? Why?
activities.insight: Bright warning colour advertises toxicity (aposematism) so predators learn, or instinctively tend, to leave it alone — the opposite strategy to camouflage, which hides. One animal survives by being SEEN, one by being HIDDEN.

checkQuestion: A poison dart frog is bright, shining red — one of the easiest things to spot in the whole forest. If bright colours make it so easy for predators to see, why on earth would a frog be coloured that way? Tell me why, and then tell me how that's different from a leaf insect's colours.
checkAnswer: The bright colour is a WARNING, not a mistake. It advertises 'I'm poisonous — don't eat me!' (this is called aposematism), so predators learn to leave it alone. That's the opposite of a leaf insect or a well-hidden tree frog, which use camouflage — dull colours and shapes that blend in — to hide. So one animal survives by being SEEN and one by being HIDDEN.
